anchors.fact: An Irish-born New York bartender who rose from bellboy to head bartender at the Ashland House, and later wrote under the name Patrick Gavin Duffy (Oxford pdf 687; *Imbibe!* pdf 91). F1
anchors.meaning: Someone with a past in the trade, not a newcomer. Pseudonym's reason unknown: no guess.

anchors.fact: He had been out of the trade for years, in Ireland and then running rooming houses in Brooklyn (Oxford pdf 687; *Imbibe!* pdf 91–92). No year for leaving (C1). F4
anchors.meaning: The quiet years, without a date to argue over.

anchors.fact: In December 1933 he told a reporter he had watched drink coming back for three years, with little to do but look after his two houses, and so began gathering recipes, thinking of a trade whose old hands had gone (*Brooklyn Daily Eagle*, 1 Dec 1933, p. 2). F5
anchors.meaning: His own account, so it may be told as fact, as reported. He saw it coming before it came.

anchors.fact: The *Eagle* reported the book out on 1 December 1933; the publisher had announced it for 5 December, the day Repeal took effect (*Eagle* 1 Dec "out this week"; *Florida Times-Union* 10 Dec; *Joy* pdf 62). F8, F11
anchors.meaning: Ready when the moment came. Say "as the ban ended" or "by the time the ban ended"; never "days before" alone, since the announced date is the day itself (A11). Prohibition is this one date clause.
anchors.speaksTo: the right words at the right time

anchors.fact: He included the dry-era mixtures because people asked for them, but marked the wilder ones (the reporter's "more fantastic") with a small circle as ones he wouldn't recommend; a launch report says he starred the ones he thought in the best tradition (*Eagle* 1 Dec 1933; *Florida Times-Union*, 10 Dec 1933, p. 37). F7, F8
anchors.meaning: Judgement given in plain marks: structure for a confused trade, without lecturing.

anchors.fact: Wondrich ranks it among the few books that did most to bring the bar's craft back after Repeal; Oxford says it stayed in print for forty years (*Imbibe!* pdf 92; Oxford pdf 687). F13
anchors.meaning: Words others stood on, judged by others. "His book", never "his recipes".

anchors.fact: His Herald Punch: dedicated to the *New York Herald* in 1901, rye with orange, a little sugar and a little St. Croix rum, shaken and strained into a sour glass (*Imbibe!* pdf 92). F14
anchors.meaning: His one drink that caught on, given to a newspaper. Whether the Manual prints it is unchecked: never "from his book".

anchors.fact: The Manual borrowed heavily (Ensslin's 1916 book, Craddock's Savoy book), and Duffy said himself he "read up on the subject" (*Imbibe!* pdf 241; *Joy* pdf 63–64; *Eagle* 1933). F6, F12
anchors.meaning: Never "his recipes", "his words" or "from memory" for the contents. What's his: the order (by base spirit), the marks, the judgement. Ensslin and Craddock stay in the dossier.

anchors.fact: Out of the guest text: the highball claim (highball.md F8), the Sullivan–Morgan meeting, his views on women bartenders and mixed drinking, liquor as a cure (F16), "a gentleman's drink" (gendered), any recipe count.
anchors.meaning: Counterweights carried openly; none is softened into praise.

anchors.fact: Year 1933, settled by the December 1933 press (F10). *A Place Kept* says "late in 1933" for Beam: our clause is the ban ending, never "shut everything down" or "late in 1933". *Anyone Would Have* (Firefighter) owns "nobody behind the bar could make it": our story is his foresight, not the skill gap.
anchors.meaning: Apart from the siblings in wording.

anchors.fact: Ours, not Duffy's: the orange juice brought up to lime strength with citric and malic acid, Arnold's method (*LI* p. 60: 32 g citric and 20 g malic per litre of fresh juice). Plain orange juice is about 0.8% acid, lime 6% (*LI* p. 137); Arnold says orange alone isn't acidic enough for a proper sour (p. 60).
anchors.meaning: The softest thing in the glass made to hold: **our reading, signposted**. Arnold's own reason was a glut of oranges, not strength. Never "his recipe" for the riffed drink.

anchors.fact: Blood orange, if Tomás uses it: Oxford CITRIC ACID (pdf 467) gives a deep red colour and slightly acidic juice, available mainly in winter; Wondrich suggests it for the "rich orange" he can't identify (*Imbibe!* pdf 92).
anchors.meaning: Seasonal: Wren's call whether "its moment comes in its season" is worth one clause. "Rich orange" is unidentified: never say what Duffy meant.

anchors.fact: The rum: Duffy wrote "enough St. Croix to flavor"; the half ounce is Wondrich's bracket, taken from a Paris "jury" he quotes without date or source (*Imbibe!* pdf 92). Today's St. Croix rum is column-still and "nothing like" the old Santa Cruz style (Oxford pdf 1732–1733).
anchors.meaning: Never "his half ounce", never "the rum he used", never "argued" or "fixed" for the jury. A Virgin Islands rum is a style choice.

anchors.fact: Oxford lists other original recipes of his (Brandy Punch, which it says his Manual describes; the Blinker and others, pdf 687). Wondrich: the Herald Punch was the one that caught on with the public (pdf 92).
anchors.meaning: Never "his only recipe" or "the one drink that's his". The Brandy Punch is a bowl (other pours' ground): out. Whether the Manual prints the Herald Punch: unchecked (library gap).

anchors.fact: The book was loose-leaf and waterproof, with supplements promised for a year (*Florida Times-Union* and *Plain Dealer*, 10 Dec 1933). F8
anchors.meaning: Never a cloth-bound book in the image or the text.

cocktail.closingLine: Sharpen the orange before anyone's thirsty. Then say it early, while nobody else is worried.
cocktail.glassware: stemmed sour glass (about 240 ml), chilled, no ice
method: Sharpen the orange. Squeeze about 4 oranges for 250 ml of juice, on the day you'll serve it, and strain it: many navel oranges turn bitter if the juice sits. Weigh in 3.4 g of citric acid and 2.1 g of malic acid, and stir until both have dissolved. If you only have citric acid, use 5.5 g. If your scale only weighs whole grams, make twice as much: 500 ml of juice, from about 8 oranges, with 11 g of citric acid. Keep it in the fridge until the first drink.
Chill the glass in the freezer, or fill it with ice water while you mix.
Put 60 ml of the sharpened juice and the sugar in a shaker, and stir until the sugar has dissolved.
Add the rye and the rum, fill the shaker with ice, and shake hard for about 12 seconds, until the outside is frosty.
Empty the glass. Strain the drink into it, through a small sieve as well so no chips of ice get in.
Hold a strip of orange peel over the drink, skin side down, and squeeze it so its oils fall on the top. Then lay it on the rim.
cocktail.name: The Long View

recipe.item: Virgin Islands (St. Croix) rum, lightly aged
recipe.note: a style; Duffy asked only for enough to flavour it, and half an ounce is Wondrich's measure. Any lightly aged rum of about 40%, not spiced
fresh orange juice with a little citric and malic acid stirred in (see step 1); in winter, try blood oranges

cocktail.tagline: The worse it gets, the clearer you are.

reading.epigraph: Rye and orange, after a bartender whose book came out as the ban ended.
whoYouAre: On an ordinary day you can seem like too much. You take the long view when the rest of the room is busy with the week, and you mention what could go wrong before anyone else is worried. People nod, and talk about something else. Then the worst day comes, the one where everyone else is lost for words, and they all look at you. You've had the words for a while.

You don't say how much the quiet stretches sting. Seeing it coming isn't much comfort while nobody's listening. And part of you, a part you'd rather not mention, steadies in a crisis, because at last you make sense. What you lie awake over is being the one in charge on the day the storm wins, and being remembered for that. So you work out what you'd say long before anyone asks, and on the day people have nothing left to stand on, you hand them a sentence that holds. People get through their worst days because of how you talk them through it.
yours: In the 1890s, Patrick Duffy was head bartender of New York's Ashland House. Someone at the time described his waxed moustache and the carnation in his lapel. Then he left the trade. Years later he was running rooming houses in Brooklyn.

In December 1933 he told a reporter how his book came about. He'd been watching drink coming back for three years, and with not much to do but look after his two houses, he'd started gathering the recipes. The book was on sale by the time the ban ended, and it holds the detail I love most. The mixtures people had got used to in the dry years went in, because people asked for them, but the wilder ones got a little circle: he wouldn't want it said he'd recommended them. The ones he thought belonged to the best tradition got a star. A cocktail historian puts it among the few books that did most to bring the craft back.

Maybe the circles were only good manners. I like to think they were more than that: a man who knew the day had come, cared what would be said about it afterwards, and made sure nobody could say he'd let it slide. You'd have drawn those circles too. You know a moment like that gets remembered, and you want to be remembered for what you stood behind.

The cocktail I've made for you starts from his Herald Punch, the one drink of his that caught on, which he dedicated to a newspaper, the *Herald*, in 1901: rye, orange juice, a spoon of sugar and just enough rum to flavour it, shaken well and strained into a sour glass. The same historian calls it a corker. Orange on its own is too gentle to hold a sour up, so I sharpen the juice, about halfway to lime, with a little of the acids that make lemons and apples tart. You still taste orange, bright and fresh, with the rye's dry spice through the middle and the rum warm underneath. It just holds. I did that as a nod to the work he did before anyone needed it.

The quiet years aren't the wait. They're where the words come from. Next time you see something coming and nobody's listening, mention it anyway, once, plainly, and early. You don't need everything to go wrong to be worth hearing. And if the day does come, you'll find people already listening.
